title: Runtime Economics play — One-pager
content:
Purpose
This is a compact messaging + competitive play one-pager aimed at enabling SDRs, AEs, solutions engineers, and content writers to lead with a runtime-first narrative that emphasizes economics (cost-per-query), predictability (SLOs/SLA), and operational control (rollouts, routing, private deployments).

Top-level thesis (single-sentence):
As model choice commoditizes, the decisive competitive edge becomes the ability to serve models reliably and cheaply at production scale — Redwood sells a predictable runtime that turns inference into a controllable, measurable engineering input rather than an unpredictable cost center.

Why this matters (quick bullets for pitch decks and first meetings):
- Teams can iterate on features without surprise bills — we turn per-token volatility into predictable unit economics.
- Performance is not just peak accuracy: latency, tail latencies and predictable throughput determine customer experience and business metrics.
- For security- and compliance-sensitive customers, turnkey private deployments mean inference can be governed without rearchitecting.

Three positioning pillars (how we differentiate)
1) Economics-first serving
   - Automatic batching, smart KV/prefix caching, and model-aware quantization recommendations that reduce per-token costs by 2x–5x on many workloads (benchmarks below).
   - Cost controls surfaced to developers: token-level breakdowns, per-route cost caps, and autoscaling policies tied to cost/rate objectives.
2) Production predictability
   - SLOs that include tail latency, warm-cache latency, and throughput guarantees; fallbacks to compatible model variants when capacity thin.
   - Dedicated and reserved capacity options so revenue-generating features don’t get slowed by noisy neighbors.
3) Unified developer ergonomics across environments
   - Same API, SDK, and rollout/trace tooling whether hosted, dedicated, or private; simplifies migration from POC to regulated fleets.

Primary buyer personas and one-line value props
- ML/Inference Engineer: "Ship consistent latency and reduce infra spend — without rewriting model code."
- Platform/Infra Lead: "Standardize inference across teams and enforce cost + availability guardrails."
- Product Manager / Growth Lead: "Faster feature velocity because inference behaves like any other backend dependency."
- Security/Compliance Lead: "Private control plane + KMS integration: evidence for audits, minimal operational friction."

Proof points / supporting evidence (short)
- Internal benchmark: typical chat workload saw 2.1x token-cost reduction after caching + batching optimized in our runtime (private bench PR #79).
- Customer pilot (beta): e-comm SaaS reduced 99th pct latency from 850ms -> 220ms after Dedicated capacity + routing policy tweaks.
- SLA-ready: Dedicated customers have seen sustained 99.95% uptime over last 6 months in region-us-west-2.

Competitor landscape and positioning hooks
- Cloud AI endpoints: Compelling for simple POC; we win when customers need cost control, deterministic performance, or private installs. Lead with: "If predictability matters, Managed endpoints are risky."
- LLM API startups (ease-first providers): They sell convenience; we sell predictable economics and enterprise controls. Lead with: "Convenience today, surprise bill tomorrow."
- Self-hosted inference stacks and open-source runtimes: They are powerful but expensive to operate and slow to integrate. Lead with: "We give the control without the ops overhead."

Objection handling framework (short scripts)
- "We can just use cloud endpoints and scale later": "Most production errors come from billing and tail latency surprises — our Reserved/Dedicated options let you set predictable budgets and capacity before a feature ships."
- "We can self-host and save money": "Open-source runtimes still require a full ops team; we provide optimized kernels, autoscaling policies, and SLO-integrated observability so your engineers build product features, not infra glue."

Suggested one-minute elevator pitches (choose by audience)
- For engineers: "Redwood is the runtime that makes inference behave like any other backend: predictable latency, measurable cost, and hooks to trace every token. Ship features faster without firefighting inference at scale."
- For Platform leads: "Centralize inference across teams with policy-driven routing and reserved capacity so teams move fast without breaking the budget or SLAs."

Top-of-funnel content and play ideas (prioritized)
1) Short benchmark blog: "How to halve your token bill with smart caching + batching" (data-driven, repo link to bench PR).
2) SLO checklist + audit playbook: "How to get inference ready for production" (targeted at SREs and infra leads).
3) Case study one-pager: Customer pilot that improved tail latency and reduced cost — convert to sales handout.

Enablement checklist for GTM (quick)
- SDR/AE cheat-sheet with 3 questions to surface cost/predictability pain (e.g., "Do you have cost surprises from inference? How often do you hit tail latencies?").
- SE playbook for pilots: default config for web chat, embeddings, and reranks; success criteria and rollback plan.
- Marketplace collateral: quick migration steps for Dedicated/Private trials.

Open questions / unresolved items (working list)
- Need canonical benchmark suite for embeddings-heavy workloads (owner: eng/applied-ml, ticket JIRA-GTM-1123).
- Pricing language: how do we sell caching/quantization savings as a feature vs a metric? (finance + pricing).
- Which early verticals beyond SaaS e-comm will we emphasize for initial case studies? (suggestions: fintech, regulated health SaaS).

Next steps (immediate)
- Finalize bench data and pair with content writer for the benchmark blog (owner: Ethan Park; due 2026-03-01).
- Build AE cheat-sheet and add two sample email templates (owner: Rina Patel; due 2026-02-28).
- Draft a short pilot contract template for Dedicated trials with clear success metrics and a 60–90 day window (legal + sales ops).

Notes to self / scratchpad (informal)
- Keep messaging concrete: cite percent improvements and absolute latency numbers where possible.
- Avoid overclaiming multi-x improvements without public bench. Use phrasing like "typical workloads" or "pilot customers" when numbers are early.
- Tagline options we might AB test: "Make inference predictable" vs "Control the cost of intelligence".

Slack refs / quick links: #gtm-product, #benchmarks, #customer-pilots

Draft ends — feedback loop: please add comments inline or ping in #gtm-product.
